title: São Paulo (state)
wiki_lead:
São Paulo (, Portuguese: [sɐ̃w ˈpawlu] ) is one of the 26 states of the Federative Republic of Brazil and is named after Saint Paul of Tarsus. It is located in the Southeast Region and is bordered by the states of Minas Gerais to the north and northeast, Paraná to the south, Rio de Janeiro to the east, and Mato Grosso do Sul to the west, in addition to the Atlantic Ocean to the southeast. It is divided into 645 municipalities. The total area is 248,219.481 square kilometres (95,838.077 square miles), comprising 2.9% of Brazil's territory. Its capital is the municipality of São Paulo, which is the most populous city in the country.
With more than 44 million inhabitants in 2022, São Paulo is the most populous Brazilian state, comprising around 22% of the Brazilian population. It is the world's 28th-most-populous sub-national entity, the most populous sub-national entity in the Americas, and the fourth-most-populous political entity of South America, surpassed only by the rest of the Brazilian federation, Colombia, and Argentina. The local population is one of the most diverse in the country. Ethnic groups present in the state include Portuguese, who colonized Brazil;  Italians, who began immigrating to the country in the late 19th century; Indigenous peoples, many distinct ethnic groups; Africans, who were brought from Africa as enslaved people in the colonial era and migrants from other regions of the country. Arabs, Armenians, Chinese, Germans, Greeks, Japanese, Spanish, and American Southerners are some other national backgrounds present in the local population.
The region of São Paulo was inhabited by Indigenous peoples from approximately 12,000 BC. In the early 16th century, the coast was visited by Portuguese and Spanish explorers and navigators. In 1532, Martim Afonso de Sousa founded São Vicente, which was the first permanent Portuguese settlement in the Americas. In the 17th century, the paulistas bandeirantes intensified the exploration of the colony's interior, which eventually expanded the territorial domain of the Portuguese Empire in South America; this would later result in the state being nicknamed the "Bandeirante State". In the 18th century, after the establishment of the province of São Paulo, the region began to gain political power, and after independence in 1822, São Paulo became a major agricultural producer in the newly constituted Empire of Brazil (mainly coffee). It developed a wealthy regional rural oligarchy over the course of the 19th century, which would shared control of the Brazilian government with the elites of Minas Gerais during the early republican period in the 1890s. Under the Vargas Era, the state was one of the first to initiate a process of industrialization and became one of the most urbanized regions of the federation.
São Paulo's economy is large and diversified, accounting for around 31% of Brazil's total wealth. It is the centre of industrial, scientific and technological production in Brazil, and is the world's largest producer of orange juice, sugar and ethanol. If it were a sovereign state, its nominal GDP would be the 21st largest in the world (2020 estimate). São Paulo is also a major tourist destination in Brazil, and has multiple sites inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Among all Brazilian states, it has the second-highest Human Development Index (HDI), the fourth GRDP per capita, the second-lowest infant mortality rate, the third-highest life expectancy, the lowest homicide rate, and the third-lowest rate of illiteracy.
